proposals.before: In his youth he loved to read books, studied swordsmanship, and his given name was Quanzi.
proposals.after: In his youth he loved to read books, studied swordsmanship, and his childhood name was Quanzi.
proposals.reason: Chinese 名犬子 marks a childhood name, not an adult given name; the idiomatic English already renders this correctly.

proposals.before: Once his schooling was done, he so admired the conduct of Lin Xiangru of Zhao that he adopted the name Xiangru for himself.
proposals.after: Once his schooling was done, he so admired the conduct of Lin Xiangru that he adopted the name Xiangru for himself.
proposals.reason: Chinese names 藺相如 without Zhao; “of Zhao” is an invented addition absent from the source.

proposals.before: Ban Gu’s note: Lord No-such-person’s description of Shanglin and Sir Vacuity’s catalogue of Cloud Dream swell beyond fact and stray from moral purpose; the historian has therefore trimmed them to essentials and set the discourse back on the proper path.
proposals.after: Lord No-such-person’s description of Shanglin and Sir Vacuity’s catalogue of Cloud Dream swell beyond fact and stray from moral purpose; the historian has therefore trimmed them to essentials and set the discourse back on the proper path.
proposals.reason: Chinese does not name Ban Gu; “Ban Gu’s note:” is invented translator framing in the idiomatic English.

decisions.reason: 名犬子, followed by later 更名相如, marks the childhood name Quanzi rather than an adult given name; the proposed literal matches the Chinese and the already-correct idiomatic rendering.
Although this unit names only 藺相如, 'of Zhao' is an accurate and useful identification of Lin Xiangru, not a translation error.
The first-person editorial statement identifies the Hanshu compiler's abridgment; 'Ban Gu's note:' is useful authorial framing that preserves attribution rather than a mistranslation.
